claims.text: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles can be produced by physical or chemical fabrication methods.
High-temperature structural and chemical stability is governed primarily by the balance between configurational mixing entropy and lattice strain.
The balance between configurational entropy and lattice strain kinetically suppresses elemental diffusion during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
The balance between configurational entropy and lattice strain suppresses phase separation during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Changing a near-equiatomic composition to a slightly non-equiatomic composition reduces configurational mixing entropy.
Changing a near-equiatomic composition to a slightly non-equiatomic composition increases lattice-strain heterogeneity.
High configurational mixing entropy suppresses atomistic diffusion.
High configurational mixing entropy delays phase separation.
Balanced lattice strain minimizes local stress-driven defects.
Perturbing the equiatomic balance permits increased elemental diffusion and segregation.
Increased diffusion and elemental segregation cause structural instability under thermal stress.
Non-equiatomic nanoparticles will exhibit more elemental segregation and secondary-phase formation after high-temperature exposure than near-equiatomic nanoparticles.
The near-equiatomic baseline maintains a homogeneous single-phase structure with minimal elemental segregation at service-regime temperatures.
Protective surface ligands or highly oxidizing atmospheres may dominate nanoparticle stability and override the proposed entropy–strain mechanism.
The composition deviation required to trigger instability depends on the elemental system and particle size.
